summary: The opening follows the playbook (one red word on frame 0, the refrain spoken at 1.45 s and said twice), but for its first 1.33 s the frame is one noun and three dots with nobody in it: put the unlit window on frame 0 and bring the faint line in by 0.5 s.

findings.criterion: the first words and the first picture
findings.ours: beat 'title', 0.00-1.33 s: on screen the single word "home", large, dark red, on a bare sheet, with "the first three dots of the road" low in the left margin; no voice. Beat 'ask', 1.45-3.08 s, first spoken words: "Text me when you're home."
findings.reference: barsat-song 0.00 s: the one-word title ("rain") in the only colour on the page beside a finished stippled drawing of two crying eyes with four tear trails (hook.jpg, all 12 frames identical). First sung words at 13.4 s, a six-word plea not to leave. patterns.md Hook: "Make the first frame name the feeling before any word is heard. One word ... and one drawn detail."
findings.why_it_matters: the words are specific: a thing people actually say, addressed to "you", not a greeting or a topic. The picture is the gap. The reference's frame 0 is a word plus a drawing that reads at once as a person and a feeling; ours is a word plus three dots that read as nothing yet, so for 1.33 s (44% of the three seconds) a stranger has one common noun on an almost empty sheet. The playbook asks for the word and the drawn detail together; ours has only the word

findings.ours: beat 'ask', 1.45-3.08 s: "Text me when you're home." The question it can open: who is saying this to me, and what is behind it? script.json question: "Why does the speaker keep asking you to text when you're home?" Answered by beat 'asking', 17.58-19.06 s: "Asking is how I love you."
findings.reference: barsat-song: no question in words in the first 3 s (benchmarks.json hook.question_opened; on the Do not copy list). Its first sung line at 13.4 s is a plea not to leave, which opens "does the person stay?" by itself because someone is already going. patterns.md Holding attention: "Open the question in the first sung line."
findings.why_it_matters: it is the same question the video answers, and it is opened in the first spoken line 12 s sooner than the reference manages. But heard once, the line is an everyday request a viewer can take at face value; the "keeps asking" in the script's question only exists from the repeat at 4.73 s, and the doubt about why from 'fine' at 14.42 s. The reference's first line carries its conflict inside it; ours does not. Inside 3 s the hook works by recognition ("someone says this to me"), and nothing in words or picture yet tells the viewer there is more behind the line

findings.ours: beats 'title' and 'ask', 0.00-3.08 s: a speaker and a "you" are implied by the address; neither is pictured. The picture is the word "home" and a road that "has left the margin and climbs a little to the right". The one sign that somebody is waiting, the lit window, first appears in beat 'light' at 11.21 s (47% of the run).
findings.reference: barsat-song 0.00 s: two crying eyes, cropped with no face, put a person and a loss on frame 0; the first sung line (13.4 s) says what is at stake, someone leaving.
findings.why_it_matters: the stakes here are small and warm by design (somebody wants to know you got home), and beat 'fine' honestly says there is no danger, so they must not be inflated. What is missing is the somebody: for the first 11 s nothing on the sheet stands for the person who is asking, where the reference shows a person in its first frame. The script already owns the right image and holds it back until nearly half-way

findings.ours: timing.json (built-in voice, pace 0.8): first picture 0.00 s ("home" is "there in frame 0", no blank, no fade-in); first word 1.45 s; first line ends 3.08 s, so 4 words are complete inside 3 s and the fifth, "home", is being spoken as the third second ends (estimated from the caption cut at 2.342 s; timing.json has no single-word times); first change of picture other than dots at 1.33 s, when the faint line arrives; first word lit at 1.45 s.
findings.reference: benchmarks.json hook: first_word_s 1.4 to 2.2 (a scaled allowance, not a measurement; the reference's own figure is 13.36 s and is a fault), first_picture_s 0.0, words_in_first_3s 0 (a fault: "a hook that opens no question in words"), first_cut_s null (the reference never changes).
findings.why_it_matters: first picture matches the reference at 0.0 s; the voice enters at the fast end of the allowed range, 11.9 s sooner than the reference; the whole refrain is heard inside about 3.1 s where the reference has no word at all. The 1.33 s before the line arrives is within the allowance, but it is the slowest stretch of the opening and the picture gives it little to do (see the first finding)

findings.ours: 0.00 s: "home" in red, readable with no sound. 1.33 s: the line "Text me" / "when you're home" is on screen whole in faint ink (carries_through.sync_rule: "so it can be read ahead with the sound off"), then lights word by word 1.45-3.08 s. The hook line is therefore fully readable without the voice, provided the faint state is legible; the script does not say how faint. Note: timing.json's automatic captions cut the same line differently ("Text me when" / "you're home.") from the script's rows ("Text me" / "when you're home").
findings.reference: barsat-song 0.00 s: the title card reads fully muted (hook.jpg), but none of its roughly 160 sung words is ever shown. benchmarks.json hook.works_muted is true as the brief's requirement, not the reference's behaviour. The reference shows no lyric, so there is nothing to compare the faint-then-lit setting against; it is judged against brief.md, Lyric sync.
findings.why_it_matters: a muted viewer gets the title word at once and the whole first line by 1.33 s, which is the brief's requirement and more than the reference gives at any point. Two things can still break it in production: faint ink too pale to read at phone size, and the automatic captions being drawn over the lyric line, which would double the words and break the rows

findings.ours: a one-word title card in the only colour on the page at frame 0, which becomes the last word of the first lyric line; the refrain is stated first (1.45 s) and repeated at once (beat 'again', 4.73 s).
findings.reference: benchmarks.json hook.type: "a complete title card at frame 0: the song's one-word title in the only colour on the page, beside a stippled ink drawing of two crying eyes; no sung word and no motion in the first 3 s". barsat-song repeats its first line at once (13.4-16.5 s and 16.8-20.2 s).
findings.why_it_matters: it is the reference's kind of opening with its listed faults removed: the title is tied to the words in time (spoken about 2.7 s after it appears, against about 87 s), the voice enters at 1.45 s against 13.36 s, and the frame moves. The one part of the reference's card it leaves out is the half that made that card readable: the drawing

findings.ours: the opening promises a quiet piece, spoken to "you", about being asked to text when you are home. Beat 'asking' (17.58 s, 74% to 80% of the run) answers why: "Asking is how I love you." Beat 'home' returns the refrain and ends on the red word, the finished road and the lit window.
findings.reference: barsat-song: the title is on screen at 0.00 s and apparently not sung until about 87-90 s, with nothing in the picture marking it (patterns.md Structure, Do not copy); its question opens at 13.4 s and is answered at about 73-77 s (tentative).
findings.why_it_matters: nothing in the opening overstates what follows: no danger is implied and none is delivered, and the word shown on frame 0 is the word the piece ends on

fixes.change: Put the window on frame 0 so the first picture has a readable drawn thing and somebody to be asking. In beat 'title', add to the picture: far right, at the height the road will end, a small window drawn as a square outline of sparse stipple dots, unlit, already there on frame 0. Then change beat 'light' from the window appearing to the window lighting: on the word "light" the dots of the dark gather round the square and thicken through the breath until the bare paper inside reads as lit. This keeps the change on "light", gives the frame the reference's layout (type left, drawing right), and makes the opening ask in picture what the lyric asks in words: a road setting out toward a window, does it get there? The close already answers it (the last dot reaches the sill on "home"). Do not change the first line and do not add any threat or worry to it.

Bring the faint first line in by 0.5 s instead of 1.33 s. In beat 'title', change the motion to: "home" stands alone on frame 0; at about 0.5 s the words "Text me" and "when you're" arrive in faint ink in their places in front of it and stay. The voice still enters at 1.45 s and lights them, so timing.json and the 1.45 s first word do not change. A muted viewer then has the whole hook line about 0.8 s sooner and the frame changes inside the first half second.

Fix the faint-ink state as a tested value, not a mood: unlit lyric words must be readable on the cream ground at phone size in a still at 1.4 s (before any word is lit). Start at about 35% to 40% of full ink and go no paler; show the unlit and lit states side by side on the board. The reference gives no value for this (it shows no lyric), so the test is legibility, per brief.md Lyric sync.

Do not pass timing.json's captions to Film.captions. The lyric line is the caption; drawing both doubles the words in the first three seconds. Take word times from transcribe.py on vo.wav for the lighting, and break the first line as the script sets it, "Text me" over "when you're home", not as the automatic captions cut it ("Text me when" / "you're home."). Also keep the bed under 0.00-1.45 s at the level it has under the first two lines: thin in texture is what the script asks, but not quieter (the reference's intro sits about 10 dB down and is on the Do not copy list).

evidence: One reference. It has public numbers (1,938,059 views, 5,421 likes, 89 comments, a 700-follower channel, as of 2026-11-25) but one video gives no result evidence: these are what the reference does, not proof of what performs. The reference is NOT a lyric video: it is one still title card held for 185.33 s under a full song, with no lyric on screen at any time, no motion and no cut. Every value about how lyrics are set, timed, moved or coloured is therefore null, and the brief governs those. Tool figures are given as measured; ranged values are the single reference's figure widened about 15% either way; length follows the brief (20 to 30 s), not the reference (185.33 s). Sung-word figures rest on a low-trust transcript of singing over a band. Beyond that, for this verdict: times are from 03-script/timing/timing.json (the script spoken by the built-in voice at pace 0.8); it has beat and caption times but no single-word times, so the moment "home" is spoken is an estimate from the caption cut at 2.342 s. The reference's first frame was checked by eye on 02-analysis/barsat-song/hook.jpg. The reference's hook is weak on four points listed under Do not copy (13.36 s before the voice, a frame held unchanged, a quiet intro, no question in words), so on those the yardstick was patterns.md, Hook, not the reference. The faint-then-lit lyric setting has no reference to compare against and was judged against brief.md only; none of its fixes is a must for that reason. This is an estimate of whether the opening does what the playbook says, not a prediction of how it will perform.
